The Time has come, He thinks, despite that Time exists no longer.
The last distant light extinguishes under His watchful gaze. At His extremities are naught but thin void blacknesses, the stars gone. Amidst space, His half-immaterial body is the lone existence that remains, stretching to infinity, drifting without destination. Ere people had proclaimed Him the end of a cycle; now in this moment He truly is. All else has passed on from being; only He persists.
So, what next?
He gazes at His own body. The blood kin He once migrated with. The kin He led to blot out countless millions upon millions of lives, all turned part of His body, nourishment for it. Where once clamored countless visions of the future, now lapsed into eternal silence. All this the cost for His life in this very moment, yet in this very moment He knows not what He could use His life for.
In yore He had a calling that drove Him to engulf those millions upon millions of lives, and each and every star and satellite they perched on, becoming as every lifeform that had and could have existed in this universe, ultimately drove Him to this shore of oblivion—yet now that once-irresistible calling grows imperceptible, soon to dwindle to nothing. Those hopes that all came to dwell within Him died at the moment where all fell quiet. Even the ones who first blessed Him with this mission may never have imagined this future to follow.
He feels lost, uneasy. But nowhere can He seek the answers. Beyond Him is mere void, and within Him purposeless nutrients. Given this, the only place to send His thought can be into the deepest recesses of His body, to stir those aimless nutrients, to try and derive the slightest hint from them.
Under His thought's interference, they begin to collide, begin to reconstitute, reform as endless and strange shatterings of information, shatterings that pass away in a blink. So in this Timeless eternity He keeps trying and trying, until His thought finally catches with nimbleness upon a piece altogether familiar to Him—it is a fragment of His own voice, metal threads' vibrations and living membranes' tremors in common harmony... Yes, it is Song.
Once, a lone technician had sung this. No matter what seas she swam, it was by herself, trailing hundreds upon thousands of optical cables behind her. The technician deftly strummed these optical cables, and amidst swirling halos sang to schools of indifferent fins that passed her by.
Once, a lone wandering singer had sung this too. No matter what lands she walked, it was by herself, trailing tune after tune of memories behind her. The singer wove those memories into ditties, and in rundown inns sang to crowds of indifferent souls.
In this moment He Himself is lone, trailing every breadth of creation He engulfed behind Him, drifting through a dying universe to the ends of Time. So in this moment, should He not sing too, to those indifferent nutrients within His body?
Skadi certainly would. While complex problems still lay on her mind to puzzle through, her Song would well forth—for Song was her language, her imagination, her creation.
So Skadi begins to sing. And in her Song, Skadi begins to blossom, more fiercely and ardently than any life that has ever blossomed before. Dimly, Skadi realizes the act she is about to undertake. With the beginning of this Song, those indifferent nutrients within her body will birth new existence, new life, a new universe.
Violently her body expands, and rapidly her consciousness scatters, and filled with hope she imagines the brand new universe she will never witness.

Skadi gazed down at the human cowering in a shell amongst the corals, trying to catch Her attention with a translation machine.
She had seen her before. The humans had built a forest of metal on the ocean floor, and she was their leader. The woman was excitedly telling Skadi about her vision—
Depart Terra for the void, in search of another Terra to migrate to. All She needed to do was accept a little bit of modification, and carry some cargo as well as humans.
The proposal was short on conflict, but suited Her nature and principles quite well.
Why refuse the offer of a greater expanse to explore and migrate to?
Following the human's guidance, Skadi swam towards the forest of metal. Her kin were waiting for Her in the steel-rimmed garden.
......
Like Her kin, Skadi was given a name: Ishar'mla, a transliteration of the name of an ancient deity of legend. They called it a Leviathan, which Skadi first took to be the humans' name for the gods of the sea. But the woman pointed at the void above the sea, and told Her that humanity considered it to also be a part of the ocean's history. God of the void sea. Skadi pondered the concept for a long time, and the sweet aftertaste lingers in Her mind even now.
......

When the woman delivered the technologically-bred 'Leviathan Offspring' to Them, Skadi found that these were no Elves. Instead, these beings took after Their image, and they were called the Seaborn. ......

The forest of metal fell silent. Only she remained, the woman who had seemed to be preparing for something ever since receiving a letter. Finally, she summoned us.

She would inject herself with a serum that would kill her, and we were to partake of her flesh. The serum would communicate all of her knowledge to us without reservation, and wipe the remnants of humanity from our memories forever.
...Lu.
She gave us no opportunity to argue. The needle pierced her neck, and she fell upon the grave she had planted for herself.
I saw her lips switch and her eyes lose focus. The only thing I heard was her final blessing.
Survive—
Survive...
Survive.

In front of her is her new office.
Two guards from Defense flank her while carrying her luggage, as is standard for a VIP escort.
Yes. Now, she too is a Very Important Person.
It's on the floor directly below Control's, sprawling with all manner of administrative and executive offices. Not that she's at all a stranger to this place, but today, it suddenly hits her that the AC is a little chilly, that her shoes are very loud against the floor, and that the looks the others give her... are harshly incisive.
She involuntarily lets out a sigh.
From behind, one of the Defense employees looks at her and sees someone who began worrying for the future of Rhine Lab the moment she assumed her post, and he can't help but feel a level of respect for her.
At that precise moment, his terminal rings. It's a notice; he quietly says a few words in response and hangs up.
'What's going on?'
'It's nothing. Apparently someone sent something through Engineering's lines. My colleagues are tracing it down; no need for you to worry.'
In short order, they arrive at the office. The Defense personnel spend a few seconds operating the door like second nature, then give her the universal handsign for 'go ahead.'
'Authenticated. Welcome, Components Control Executive Consultant Olivia Silence.'
She opens the door and enters.
The Defense personnel place her luggage on the coffee table, then take their leave at her nod.
She surveys her surroundings. A large, standard office, so empty that Ifrit could misbehave all she wants in here, with room to spare.
Before she can let out an even deeper sigh, the door behind her opens then shuts again with no warning.
'Was there anything el—' She's suddenly compelled to swallow what she was saying, for her visitor is not a person, but—
'A Meeboo?!' Yes, in front of her, without a doubt, sits one of Mayer's proud works.
It's carrying a bag on its back, containing a pouch of coffee beans, a mug, and an accompanying letter.
She opens it. It's Mayer's handwriting.
'Boy have I been wondering what kind of gift to get you. Joyce told me she was gonna go for coffee beans, and eureka! So I remodeled one of my Meeboos a little.
'You left while I was still working on it, and I was gonna mail it to you, but then Components Control said you'd already had a mountain in your inbox, and just the ETA on inspection was half a month, and I'm not waiting that long, so I borrowed Engineering's lines a little.'
There's a knock at the door.
Dammit, thinks Silence. If they find this Meeboo—
She lifts her head and sees it jump onto her new desk and, through a series of elaborate transformations, morph into a coffee machine.
The same Defense employee as before enters apologetically. 'Sorry, Ms. Silence, whatever was sent through the pipeline apparently arrived here. Is there anything in your office that, uh, can I ask what—
'It's just a coffee machine,' Silence replies, shooting from the hip.
'But...'
'It was a gift from my friend to celebrate my promotion. Is something the matter?' Silence says, picking up the beans and pouring them into the Meeboo, before attempting to pour herself a practiced cup of coffee—er, it should be this button, she imagines? Oh, wonderful, she got it right.
'Understood. As long as there's nothing out of the ordinary. Excuse me.'
Suspicious no longer, the Defense employee turns and leaves.
She lets out a third sigh, this time of relief.
Hm. Right, the letter kept going.
'I already told you at the farewell, but you know, might as well tell you one more time. Congrats on the promotion, Silence! I promise I'll swing by next time I'm back at HQ!'
She feels herself relax a little. Some things have changed, that much is true, but other things feel like they'll never change at all.
And with this coffee machine around, she shouldn't having trouble staying awake, at least.

By the time Silence returned from the committee office to Components Control, there was already a completed project plan outlining the construction of a new observation station and S.H.A.F.T. system in Kjerag on her desk.
After the crisis that shocked everyone involved, after the expedition that drew all of Terra's attention, someone had once again proposed an invitation to the distant sky. This was bound to happen—Silence knew this day would come. After all, the stars are right there, and there was bound to be someone curious about her.
Silence spots the sharp signature on the documents, made by the last person to handle them. One month ago, this project was just one among many proposed in the Directors' meeting. Afterwards, Components Control Acting Director Saria did not consult Silence on the project, choosing instead to proceed with it as usual. Silence is unsure which of these choices Saria would have found harder to make.
Silence is well aware that the project costing tens of billions of Columbian gold certificates cannot truly begin without her own signature, not to mention the complex and innumerable procedures to follow. Such was the authority granted to her by the city and the country, the weight of which seems almost unreal.
So, should she sign it?
Kjerag, a name that is rarely brought up in Columbia, usually calls to mind the image of a snowy mountain, based on the data occasionally brought back by teams from the Scientific Investigation Section. Establishing an observation station there was bound to attract too many eyes to that country known for standing aloof from worldly affairs. But that aside, was the Rhine Lab of today even ready to take such a big step?
Political games and military ambitions—who can say that a mere scientist wouldn't be dragged into the next maelstrom of disputes between the two? What can be done to ensure the situation does not slide into the abyss of violence? No matter how perfect the rules, loopholes are inevitable. Every step forward science takes is an arduous effort, but things other than science must also factor into the equation.
There are too many factors to worry about.
Only now does Silence understand that, with the power she holds, it is far more difficult to affirm than to reject. She has already come up with many reasons to delay or even outright refuse to green light the project, but there is only a single reason to approve it.
Choosing to stand against radical ideas does not mean standing against science. More importantly, someone needs Silence by her side.
Humanity is rightly entitled to venture towards the future, and there is no perfect solution to the structural conflicts between different groups of people. But she can only choose to place her hopes on individuals.
Silence looks out the window. The skies of Trimounts are clear tonight, and she knows someone else is looking at the same sky.
She signs her name on the document.

The camera chases through a narrow alley shrouded in morning mist. The stone pavement is still damp from the previous night's rain. Momoka Hanyuu, wearing a coarse cotton haori, trots along while waving to the director holding the microphone: 'Let me finish saying hello first.'
At the alley's entrance, the first extra is an old craftsman selling kerosene lamps. He wipes his blackened palms on his apron and hands over the lamp he's just repaired. Momoka accepts it with a smile and thanks him earnestly. A little farther on is the young man who owns the bookshop. He's just been selected as a second extra. He stands under a weather-worn signboard and somewhat bashfully speaks his single line: 'Yes, my lord.' Nevertheless, Momoka painstakingly rehearses it with him again and again. The camera follows her through the corridor. The shopkeeper is simmering stew. Just as she lifts the lid, the steam bursts against the lens, and she blurts out a string of apologies. At the confectionery, the clerk gently brushes aside the children who are straining to peek in. Momoka makes a silly face at the doorway as she passes by, and everyone laughs. The boom mic keeps bumping against the low eaves, picking up the chime of wind bells and the cries of the vendors. Every single sound on the street is recorded on the tape, as the reels spin round and round.
Before filming begins in the afternoon, Momoka sits on the rear bench of a prop cart. Around her, coachmen, vendors, and apprentices hired for the day crowd in to watch as she pins up a little girl's hair. The camera lingers on a strand of loose hair at her neck, damp with sweat, then slowly pulls back. The camera sweeps across the faded lattice windows of the townhouses, the moss-covered stone lanterns, and the power lines strung like webs between the wooden houses. No one could have possibly imagined that years later all of this would be reduced to ruins in a sudden eruption of violence.
On this day, everyone is hard at work on a film that still feels underdeveloped. Laughter, chatter, and the clicking of the camera create a din that reverberates through every nook and cranny in Kajimachi.
The final scene the director films that day shows Momoka standing on a bridge over the river, holding a floral bouquet that the crew gave her to celebrate the ending of filming. She turns back around to wave directly at the camera. The sunset casts a golden edge along the brim of her hat. In the background, the extras gradually disperse, their shadows trailing behind them as they head home. No one hurries to take down the planks laid across the river, as if filming will continue tomorrow with the same scene.
That's the end of the outtake reel. Momoka's room is now silent, save for the ticking of the clock. She curls up into a ball on the sofa. On the TV screen, her younger self still stands on the bridge, waving at the camera. The river is dyed by the setting sun, thick and gleaming like boiled honey. She keeps watching for a long time, until the screen reverts back to the blue standby display. Only then does she raise the remote and switch it off. The room goes dark at once. A sliver of light peeks through from outside, faintly illuminating the small plant she keeps by her window and the faded photograph beside it—just like the sunset that slipped through the lattice windows of the old wooden house and brightened her heart so many years ago.
uniequip_002_ling:
A great wind comes from the depths of the desert, blowing straight across a boundless meadow. Beyond it is a nomadic city, its night as bright as the day.
'This wind––'
'What about it?'
'I'm not sure how to describe it right now.'
'Even the great wordsmith, Ling, has times when she's lost for words?'

The wind first passes through the eaves of the garden, swirling around the head of the willow tree. Its power largely spent, it brushes against Ling's face, as if scratching an itch.
'The company of friends, endless cups of wine. The warm wind brings me––'
'I flipped through your recent poems...' A sudden voice rings out.
'Brother...'
'Warm wind, fragrant wind, easterly wind, lotus wind, willow wind, wind across the bridge, wind beneath the fan... Why don't you try going somewhere without wind for a change?'
'Is there any place in this world that doesn't host any wind?'
She can't remember how many poetry meetings she has attended recently - pretty much the same gardens, the same meandering water, the same thousand cups of liquid you couldn't get drunk on, the same hundred poems, the same charming emotions. To make merry is fine indeed, but it is too easy to make merry.
'There may be a place that needs you more... somewhere that'll let you compose new poems.'

In order to control its only water source, this nomadic city does not rely on the mountains as a barrier, but rather stands on the vast desert, like a lonely giant in an unfathomably vast world with nobody else to rely on. The great wind rouses, occasionally kicking up rough sand and dust that passes across one's cheeks like daggers.
It's not as if there's no wind here - it's just not that same kind of wind. The mountain's sanctuary is distant, the spring wind's breath expired.
Ling stares at the meadow but a stone's throw away, where the last of the remaining elite soldiers lay, their armor covered in wet spikes. Three whole battalions, yet the meadow at night is nothing but a meadow.
An ambush took place here. The city that rouses the night was the bait, while the meadow was the trap.
'Light the torches brighter.'
'They're already bright enough to attract those guys.'
'It is for the soldiers beneath the meadow to see. War comes soon, and none shall return. Nobody can resist the urge to turn around and look. Burn them brighter, and they shall become the lights of their hometowns.'
The great wind cannot extinguish the flames in the meadow, the men's eyes fix upon their homes through the night.

A cold wind blows, the senses stir. Her eyes open to the depths of Shancheng's night. Empty jars of Husong wine fill the pavilion, a half-written poem on the page in front of her.
uniequip_002_ironmn:
A fully automatic dual-purpose passenger-freighter carrier device serving the entire landship!
Before seeing the design blueprints, none of Engineering's operators would have thought Feist had such a marvelous imagination. No wonder he'd dubbed the plans 'Dreams' and stuck them in the most eye-catching spot of his workbench.
The creativity on show in the blueprints was succinct: Preserve the motor core of an FMC, then upgrade it with an all-terrain ambulatory mechanical installation.
'How many neat automation ideas has this guy got hidden up in that head of his?' Closure was heard to say in appraisal, which served to stir up Engineering even more. Finally, one voice said what everyone was secretly thinking—
'Let's get this thing made while he's out in the field!'
Predictably they came to a resounding agreement. They'd all received Feist's help in ways both big and small, or been given one of his timely little presents. Moreover, not one operator there would ever refuse the chance to make someone's dream a reality.
Several workshops joined hands and got down to work, all of Engineering bustling like nobody's business. Driven by wanting to finish it before Feist got back, sticking points were overcome one after another, and progress flew by far smoother than usual. Very soon, the main chassis was fully built, short of just one final step: merging it with a Feist Metal Crab motor system.
Once 'MERGE SUCCESSFUL' flashed up on their giant display, ardent applause filled all of Engineering. A brand spanking new automated transport vehicle could enter operation, and it couldn't have happened without the combined hard work of Feist and every single other engineer. Some operators had already begun to imagine how he would react to seeing it: would a lad who'd pulled himself out of the fires of war shed a tear or two? Or would he laugh like mad and give everyone a giant hug?
That was when a question came that threw everyone off, its asker stood over by the generator.
'How does the FMC motor system... actually work?'
Clearly, nobody had given thought to this one little detail preserved from the design, and a moment of silence ensued that felt like forever.
'Hey, what're you lot all gathered in here for?'
Feist, who'd come back aboard earlier, gave the crowd a puzzled stare before his eyes fell on the little sheetmetal fellow they surrounded. He blinked, then blinked again, making sure he wasn't just hallucinating.
'Hold on, you got the Crawler all built? I don't know what to say!'
All of Engineering's eyes were on him as he picked up a steel pipe and gave the 'Crawler' a hefty tap on the back. With a loud rumble, the 'Crawler' slowly whirred into motion. That was the instant that reminded everyone just how the FMC operated.
A few days later, the children aboard Rhodes got the gift Stainless had promised them: a little people-carrying robot that moved when you struck it. There in the shade of a thicket of steel, both his and their dreams had come true at once.
Now they just needed to find an open space, and everyone could experience the joy of riding a burdenbeast.
uniequip_003_ironmn:
Rhodes Island has been invited to tour Highbury, which in recent times is all but the beating heart of Victorian industry. So, you, together with a convoy of operators looking forward to some exchange study, step for the first time in a while onto its formerly war-blighted soil.
All is not as you left it. No longer is Highbury crossed with heat and the sweat of brows; now, it's a well-oiled machine, the picture of order. With a grin, Stainless tells you that you've the Londinium Industry Development Association to thank—they've brought together every factory, advanced every proposal, combined every assembly line they could to produce the Highbury of today.
You don't tell him you heard as much on the factory tour you just took (you've been at this since morning, and it was your hunger that had you leave the rest of the ops to their tour while you nipped out for a bite to eat); it's been a while since you've seen Stainless talk so glowingly, and you're not about to interrupt him. You just nod along while you scan about for that smashing fried fin place he told you of the last time you were in town.
What greets you when you get there, though, is a random factory's side door. Only then in your hunger do Stainless's words register properly: the whole borough's layout got revised, which meant the fin place had to move premises. Your stomach chooses this moment to grumble loudly.
'What's that, Doctor, getting peckish? I was just going to say, that best chippy in town I told you about a while back? It's right here!'
You nod, perplexed as to why Stainless is stopping here... and opening the door to beckon you in. Is he trying to starve you?
A moment later, a giant stonking thing appears before your eyes with a thunderous boom. Stainless skips over and hops into the cockpit, and shakes you out of your stunned stupor with a yell. 'The Crawler! Doctor, I give you The Crawler!
Didn't I mention we were revising the borough layout? Well, they wanted to optimize out the food stands, up the place's total usability—but I didn't think so! Factories might define Highbury, but so do our little eateries!'
'So?' you shout back, swept along by his sudden fervor.
'So—'
With Stainless at the helm, THWOOMP! The Crawler's shell unfolds in all directions to reveal its inner workings—and what should greet you but several stands. One stand's owner in particular is frying her fins with the half an arm the war left her, and she's deft as ever. She greets you all smiles.
'How's that for a show? A decommissioned first-model Crawler! Couldn't leave it gathering dust on the factory floor, and I so happen to have a stand to run! Now it's the Nomadic Food Crawler! Look, got my hand-drawn sign up there and everything!'
You're dumbstruck, and in your dumbstruckedness climb up a Crawler leg and into the thing, and continue to be dumbstruck as Stainless guides you through ordering a whole table's worth of food. Finally, your mouth closes again around a bite of crisp golden battered fin, and you feel happiness permeate all throughout you. It's now that you see Stainless up in the Crawler's cockpit, the wind tousling his hair, and when he looks over his shoulder, your eyes meet.
'Doctor! This is a lot like that dream I told you about, right? That stupid, barmy dream.'
You nod.
He throws his arms wide open as he welcomes the wind and sun that rush to greet him. 'Doctor, I think I've made it come true.'
uniequip_002_nasti:
'Director Nasti, I heard it took you only six months to go from joining Rhine Lab to leading Engineering?'
'Three.'
'Just... three months?'
'To be precise, Rhine Lab only established an official Engineering Section after I joined, to provide engineering support for the mountain of proposals from Muelsyse, Ferdinand, and the others. I joined the company in its early days, but after it had already attracted quite a lot of attention. And given my background... you could certainly say that three months was an especially short period for a Sarkaz who showed up out of nowhere to assume a regular role here.'
'You mean the vetting process went smoothly for you?'
'One of my people over at Maylander secretly helped me out. Of course, I only found out about that later.'
'Hiding your history must have been difficult.'
'Maybe you've been spending too much time listening to water-cooler rumors. The more time you waste on this routine interview, the more time I'll have to spend later 'hiding my history', as you put it. A young company like this—a young country like this—has always derived its nutrients from age-old secrets.'
'My apologies, Director Nasti. I-I'm just a little nervous. I thought you'd have declined the interview, or responded the way Director Muelsyse did. Only halfway through my interview with her did I realize I was talking to a water clone the whole time...'
'They don't have any function like that.'
'They? Oh, you're referring to the robots by your feet? According to HR's surveys, many of our employees are very interested in them... What should we call them?'
'Branch-type fully-loaded hybrid precision work robots. Each of them bears a unique eight-digit serial number indicating the scope of their respective duties. I have incantations inscribed on their core components so they can seamlessly adhere to my commands.'
'So I take it you're like their mother, Director?'
'No. They do whatever I want. They're merely the bricks and bolts of whatever project needs them. Just like me. Also, don't casually project such precious emotions onto inanimate objects.'
'...'
'Alright, kid. You don't have to force yourself to think of any more questions to ask. Just leave the rest to me.'
—Excerpt from a Rhine Lab HR Audio Log

Thank god Director Jara showed up in the nick of time, before the mood in the room dropped below zero.
To be honest, the Director of Engineering isn't that hard to get along with, other than her schedule being difficult to squeeze into. She's just focused on efficiency and her work, and I could be myself for the most part.
The two of them soon shifted topics and began discussing Control. Probably Director Jara was subtly asking where Control was.
'This was your true motive for the interview, wasn't it?' The conversation continued, and I heard Director Nasti switch to an unusually gentler tone. 'Kristen doesn't want you to know too much. I understand her reasons, so I'll say nothing more on the matter.'
It seems like I'll never get the chance to apologize to her.
—Supplementary explanation from HR staff Jennifer
uniequip_002_cello:
Her tutor seems very late to today's lesson, but the student hardly cares. She's always hated this tutor anyway. Clearly she's good enough to finish this whole cello solo unguided! But somehow, her tutor's just never satisfied.
Certainly, she can't play as well as her tutor. Oh, she's tried to submerge herself in the score, to converse without care with the composer she never got to know. But those ebon-black markings have stayed silent on their chalk-white scores. Their mysterious composer passed away almost a century ago; they say she died all alone, and practically left no trace she ever lived save for a few of her scores. It's not in her grasp to comprehend the passion and sorrow that lie within each movement, nor does she have a clue who that 'ever-lost lover' hiding with the score really was, or why they were struck by such fits of madness.
And so she can only but play as the score instructs, emotionlessly. At first, it goes well enough. She can still feel the brush of each note, feel them settle in her heart. But as the movements progress, and the music enters its passages of true frothing turbulence, the leaps, the repeats, those elegant trills and appoggiaturas, it all embraces her with fervor. They invite her to a mad dance, but step by step, her gait follows less and less. Tempestuous crescendos and diminuendos barrel violently through her vision, only to slip away next instant to the score's furthest reaches. She tries to catch them, grab hold of each glittering moment that accompanies them, struggling in the midst of the endlessly long staff to the point her strings' tremors can no longer rouse those worked-up emotions, and their place is taken by the repetitious back-and-forth of the metronome, clack, clack, clack, clack... echoing lonely in her ears, until the impassioned music agonizingly lingers no longer, as if this betrayal was preordained.
And thus, the energy fades from her fingertips as does that beautiful passage, leaving only the metronome still chiming away. Clack, clack, clack, clack... This imperfect silence becomes a parting declaration. At this, the fury and despair that lurk in her heart burst forth, becoming the heat in the tears her eyes brim with. Her vision blurs—the plain white score before her bids her final throes of resistance. She snatches the quill, and upon the score engraves each and every leap, every repeat, every elegant trill and appoggiatura, every tempestuous crescendo and diminuendo. Jet-black like cast iron shackles, she knows she's gone mad, but this is the only way she has to bind her ever-lost lover to her side. Before the final barline ends it all, her life will flow with the music.
And this is when the cello grinds to a halt. She finds herself holding the bow, the cello silently resting upon her bosom, and the strings are not quivering, and the metronome is not rocking, and all that fills the chamber is her heavy breathing. And her Sankta tutor, with her black gloves, gently brushes a hand over hers, and speaks in the same soft and gentle tone as ever.
'Your playing today was perfect,' she congratulates her, content. 'The composer's life, and her love, flowed within your performance.'
uniequip_003_cello:
To Cardinal Sangallo, First Tribunal, CC to the Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Tribunals:
Attached please find the investigative report on the adverse impact on Sankta empathy caused by music from an unknown source in the recent calamity at Faber Central Hospital, and Executor Federico's report on Arturia Giallo's escape from captivity... All relevant files pertaining to Arturia Giallo are hereby sealed, and her citizenship privileges listed in Clauses 1 through 13 of the Laterano Constitution restored.
—Yvangelista XI
Yvangelista XI signs the letter with one hand and reaches out towards the dried cactus on the table with another. The dessert bowl on the desk was a little far away, but someone gently nudges it towards him.
'Ah, talk about timing.' The old man looks up at his visitor. 'I just signed off on a document about you.'
'A rather generous treatment, is it not?' Arturia sits down opposite the old man with a smile. 'Does the new Law permit offsetting transgressions with merit?'
'The whole city heard your performance that evening, after all... Not a particularly Lateran tune, but moving nonetheless.'
'It wasn't a particularly Lateran scene to begin with.'
'True. Incidentally, you called it 'offsetting transgressions with merit'? I was rather under the impression that you had never acknowledged your past deeds as 'transgressions'.'
'It is important for a musician to reflect on their tastes and habits from time to time.'
'Oh?'
'Someone who loves the changing clouds inevitably dislikes the monotony of sun and rain. Once, when I touched those dull and tedious voices of the heart, I felt like a cloudbeast obsessed with cleanliness falling into a pit of mud. I walked the land in search of great, dynamic souls. I visited the lost realm of the Zhayedan, the Witch King's Pavillon... missing out on thousands of other souls in the process. I know I must have passed those people by with a frown.'
'Ouch, my tooth... Go on, I'm listening.'
'But the one performance in my life I have the least regrets about was when I greeted night falling upon Laterano that day, with a group of strangers singing hymns in Bolívarian. Might I be so bold as to claim that I changed my listeners in some measure? Perhaps the dynamic changes I've been seeking all this time begin with my own fingertips. They belong to the future, not to the past.
'I want to retrace my path, Your Holiness. Perhaps I will encounter an audience I once overlooked, perhaps even those who play music without souls...'
'You mean the Seaborn?'
'Perhaps.'
'So you came to say farewell. It sounds like your path is a long one.'
'Whose isn't?' Arturia caresses the strings on her cello, as her smile grows even brighter. 'Fortunately, I have my cello.'
'That's true.'
Young and old sit opposite one another, both working their jaws hard. The conversation is over, and nothing shall interrupt this moment of tranquility. After all, the young Sankta's journey will soon begin once she is done with that piece of dried cactus.
uniequip_002_phatm2:
A misprinted Sargonian coin with an indistinct inscription on one side and a sigil of two faces facing away from each other on the other. An extremely rare find. Judging from the degree of degradation, this little thing is more than a hundred fifty years old. The collector from Toron would have been unwilling to trade it for such a low price were he not in urgent need of funds. It is also on that fortunate rainy night that I meet an unusual guest, draped in a black cloak, speaking with a unique accent from northwestern Victoria, who asks me where my gold coin came from. As I get older, it has gotten easier to wag my tongue with irrelevant gossip than to give a genuine response. I assume a young man like him will interrupt my endless preamble, but he listens with interest. My own interest grows, so I tell him my own interpretation of the special mark on the coin. Before he leaves, he tells me to let him know if I add any more relics with similar sigils to my collection, and he vanishes like a shadow into the rainy night of Londinium.
Afterward, I keep in touch with the mysterious gentleman from time to time. Even if he is unable to immediately visit my shabby shop as soon as I send word, he always comes by on a good day to listen to me tell the stories of the relics and their previous owners. As time passes, I grow curious, wondering what he is looking for. I visit some old chaps and learn that the mark has links to an ancient drama cult. Recalling my mysterious guest who always comes by late at night, I cannot help but feel a pang of worry. However, whether due to my ordinary life causing an infatuation with legends, or his silent but generous gestures alleviating my concerns, we continue to maintain a good business relationship. I can tell this gentleman is eager to collect more information about this twin-face sigil, but he also seems deeply interested in the other curios in the shop too, flipping through old, dry scripts, or admiring my latest collection of paintings on the wall whenever he stops by. He seems to be naturally drawn in by art. During one of our meetings, a ticket stub falls from his pocket, and I learn he is an actor from a wandering troupe. When I mention my interest in seeing him perform, he shakes his head and says he will never perform again. After he leaves, I turn over the stub to find a familiar mark on the paper... What a shame. My guess is that he was a brilliant actor.
Eight years pass since I first met Mr. Lucian. He has not come by in recent times, even as I get older and older. Tonight is yet another rainy night, and to my surprise, my familiar yet stranger of a customer stops by. This time he is dressed in completely different attire, and even his eyes exudes a changed air. I am momentarily stunned but manage to ask my usual 'What are you looking for, sir?' He does not answer, but takes out a brand new gold leaf from his sleeve, our tacitly understood mark engraved upon it. The leaf glows with a dynamic, newborn luster within my otherwise dusty little abode. I want to place this beautiful present in the most eye-catching spot in my shop, but the gentleman merely puts it on top of the nearest shelf, just like how a writer leaves a period in between lines to await a reader to question and interpret it. After telling the story of dozens of these sigils, I too have become a part of this story.
How wonderful, that he finally solved his own mystery.
I figure I will never see him again.
